strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in pool-based active learning (AL): no single acquisition heuristic (uncertainty, representativeness, diversity) consistently dominates across different domains, models, and AL cycles.

The proposed progressive filtering mechanism is modular, training-free, and can serve as a plug-and-play preprocessing pool-cleaning step for external downstream acquisition strategies, as convincingly demonstrated in the ESC50 audio classification use case.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 datasets and 3 modern vision foundation models (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP) with 10 independent trials per configuration, showing consistent and substantial improvements in AULC and pairwise win rates over both individual AL strategies and prior ensemble methods.

Thorough ablation studies analyzing the impact of hyperparameters (filtering rounds $R$, subsampling ratio $\alpha$, and number of batches $J$), alongside transparent discussion of failure modes (e.g., when multiple ensemble heuristics degrade below random sampling).
weaknesses: Computational overhead is significant: running $M$ strategies over $J$ subsampled iterations across $R$ rounds requires $M \times J \times R$ batch selection executions per AL cycle (e.g., $8 \times 10 \times 5 = 400$ evaluations per cycle). Although parallelization and subsampling mitigate this, the paper lacks explicit wall-clock time comparisons against standard single-pass AL baselines.

The theoretical justification in Theorem 3 relies on an overly optimistic assumption: $V(x) > V(y) \implies p_{m,r}(x) \ge p_{m,r}(y)$ for all strategies $m$. The core motivation of the paper is precisely that individual strategies often fail or have blind spots; assuming every heuristic is monotonically aligned with true value makes the monotonicity of expected pool value somewhat tautological.

The experimental scope is restricted to linear probing / head fine-tuning over frozen foundation model backbones. While standard in recent benchmarks, verifying whether progressive filtering holds under end-to-end or parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA) where representations drift between cycles remains unaddressed.

strengths: Well-motivated approach: Addressing the instability and blind spots of individual AL strategies across different budgets, models, and datasets via an ensemble filtering mechanism is conceptually sound and practically relevant.

Methodological clarity and simplicity: The two-stage framework (progressive filtering via union over subsampled rounds, followed by coverage-based selection on the refined pool) is intuitive, training-free, and agnostic to the choice of underlying selection strategies.

Theoretical foundation: The paper provides formal probabilistic bounds (Theorems 1–3) showing value preservation, exponential reduction of uninformative instances through iterative filtering, and monotonic non-decrease of expected pool value under reasonable correlation assumptions.

Thorough empirical evaluation: Extensive experiments across 6 image classification datasets (up to 200 classes) and 3 vision foundation models (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), with 10 independent trials. The results show strong improvements and high pairwise win rates over both strong individual AL strategies (e.g., UHerding, BAIT) and prior ensemble AL methods (SelectAL, TCM, TAILOR).

Insightful ablations and use-case transfer: The ablations convincingly demonstrate that progressive filtering alone elevates candidate pool quality (even for random sampling and failing strategies like BAIT on DINOv3 or Coreset on ESC50 audio spectrograms), confirming that the benefits stem from pool refinement.
weaknesses: Substantial computational overhead: In each AL cycle, running R rounds with M strategies and J batch selections per strategy requires R * M * J selections (e.g., 5 * 8 * 10 = 400 strategy evaluations per cycle). Although subsampling with ratio alpha < 1 and parallelization mitigate this, running compute-heavy strategies (such as BAIT or BADGE) repeatedly incurs non-trivial wall-clock overhead. Explicit wall-clock runtime comparisons against baselines are missing.

Evaluation restricted to linear probing / frozen backbones: All image experiments keep the foundation backbones frozen and train only the linear classification head. While this is increasingly common in foundation model regimes, it remains unclear how the method translates to partially or fully fine-tuned representations where feature distributions change across cycles.

Idealized assumptions in Theorem 3: Theorem 3 assumes that every AL strategy consistently assigns higher selection probability to instances with higher true value V(x). In practice, heuristic strategies can fall prey to outliers or misleading data points, which violates this assumption and can cause uninformative or noisy instances to be repeatedly selected (as observed on Dopanim with CLIP).

strengths: Principled and novel formulation for AL ensembling: Instead of attempting brittle algorithm selection or hard budget switching (e.g., multi-armed bandits or threshold heuristics), REFINE introduces progressive filtering to clean the unlabeled pool iteratively via union of selections, followed by coverage-based selection.

Rigorous theoretical justification: The paper provides clear probabilistic formulations and bounds demonstrating (1) high survival rates for high-value instances (Theorem 1), (2) exponential decay of uninformative instances (Theorem 2), and (3) monotonic concentration toward high-value pools under reasonable ranking conditions (Theorem 3).

Extensive empirical benchmark: Evaluated across 6 image classification benchmarks, 3 modern foundation models (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), and an audio domain application (ESC-50), demonstrating consistent improvements over 8 competitive individual AL strategies and 3 existing ensemble methods.

Agnostic preprocessing capability: The progressive filtering stage effectively boosts the performance of individual AL heuristics (including simple random sampling and CoreSet) when applied prior to selection, highlighting its modular utility.

Honest analysis of limitations: The authors transparently analyze cases where the ensemble degrades (e.g., Dopanim with CLIP) and discuss the sensitivity of the method to ensemble quality and diversity.
weaknesses: Computational overhead and lack of wall-clock runtime analysis: Applying $M$ strategies over $J$ subsamples across $R$ rounds requires $M \times J \times R$ strategy calls per cycle (e.g., $8 \times 10 \times 5 = 400$ calls). Even with subsampling ratio $\alpha$ and parallel execution, compute-intensive AL strategies (such as BAIT or BADGE) can add significant latency. Reporting wall-clock times and FLOPs relative to baseline methods would clarify practical deployment feasibility.

Evaluation restricted to frozen backbones (linear probing): The experiments only evaluate linear classification heads on top of frozen foundation models. It remains unclear how progressive filtering interacts with end-to-end fine-tuning or parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA), where representations evolve dynamically between AL cycles.

Strong assumption in Theorem 3: Theorem 3 assumes that for all strategies $s_m$, $V(x) > V(y) \implies p_{m,r}(x) \ge p_{m,r}(y)$. In practice, complementary strategies often evaluate orthogonal or contradictory criteria (e.g., representative density vs. boundary uncertainty often negatively correlate for outliers), making this assumption idealistic.

strengths: Novel and intuitive framework: Rather than committing to a single strategy or learning complex heuristic selectors, REFINE utilizes a two-stage approach—iterative progressive filtering via unions of candidate batches followed by coverage-based selection—to effectively clean the unlabeled pool and capture diverse notions of data value.

Solid theoretical support: The manuscript provides rigorous probabilistic bounds demonstrating value preservation (Theorem 1), exponential reduction of uninformative instances (Theorem 2), and non-decreasing expected pool value (Theorem 3).

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: Evaluated across 6 image classification benchmarks, 3 foundation backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), and an audio spectrogram task, consistently outperforming both 8 strong individual AL strategies and 4 state-of-the-art ensemble methods over multiple runs.

Modular utility as a preprocessor: The experiments demonstrate that progressive filtering can serve as an effective, workflow-agnostic preprocessing step that boosts the performance of arbitrary downstream AL selection strategies (including Coreset and BAIT).
weaknesses: Computational overhead of repeated acquisitions: Progressive filtering requires evaluating $M$ strategies across $J$ subsamples over $R$ rounds per AL cycle ($M \times J \times R$ calls per cycle). While parallelization and subsampling ratio $\alpha$ mitigate this, the cumulative computational cost remains substantially higher than standard single-strategy active learning.

Strong assumption in Theorem 3: Theorem 3 assumes that all strategies $s_m$ are monotonically aligned with the unknown true instance value ($V(x) > V(y) \implies p_{m,r}(x) \ge p_{m,r}(y)$), which is rarely guaranteed in real-world scenarios where strategies fail or select adversarial/outlier points.

Vulnerability of union operation to poor ensemble members: Taking the union means that if multiple constituent strategies produce poor or noisy selections, uninformative samples easily propagate into the candidate pool (as noted in the Dopanim CLIP experiment).
Minor presentation omission: In Section 5, the sentence 'Our implementation can be found at' is left incomplete without a placeholder or anonymized URL.

strengths: Compelling motivation and intuitive framework: The paper tackles a well-documented failure mode in active learning—the sensitivity and cycle-dependent instability of individual heuristics—by proposing a simple, training-free ensemble approach that avoids hard strategy switching.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across six vision datasets, three modern foundation models (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), and multiple downstream scenarios (class imbalance, distribution shift, partial fine-tuning, and audio classification). Experiments are run over 10 independent trials and benchmarked against both strong individual strategies (e.g., UHerding, BAIT) and modern ensemble baselines (e.g., AutoAL, TAILOR).

Versatility of progressive filtering: The authors convincingly show that progressive filtering functions as an effective standalone pool-cleaning pre-processing step, improving downstream performance across various acquisition functions (including random sampling and Coreset).

Solid theoretical framing: Theorems 1, 2, and 3 provide useful analytical bounds and conceptual intuition for why iterative union filtering retains informative instances while exponentially decaying the survival probability of uniformly low-utility samples.
weaknesses: Substantial computational overhead: In each AL cycle, running $M$ strategies across $J$ draws over $R$ rounds requires up to $M \times J \times R$ acquisition passes (e.g., $8 \times 10 \times 5 = 400$ passes per cycle). While subsampling ($\alpha < 1$) and parallelization mitigate runtime, this remains considerably more compute- and memory-intensive than standard AL methods.

Strong assumption in Theorem 3: The proof of monotonically non-decreasing expected pool value relies on the assumption that every strategy $s_m \in \mathcal{S}$ is strictly monotonic with respect to true instance utility ($V(x) > V(y) \implies p_{m,r}(x) \ge p_{m,r}(y)$). In practical deep active learning, individual heuristics frequently prioritize outliers, mislabeled samples, or uninformative hard negatives.

Sensitivity to poor ensemble members: As acknowledged by the authors in the Dopanim (CLIP) experiment, if multiple constituent strategies perform poorly or choose redundant/noisy regions, progressive filtering retains these samples via the union operator without an adaptive weighting mechanism to downweight failing strategies.

strengths: Conceptual novelty: Shifting the perspective of ensemble active learning from choosing/weighting specific strategies to progressive pool cleaning/filtering via the union of expert selections is intuitive and effective.

Theoretical foundation: The authors support progressive filtering with formal theoretical analysis (Theorems 1-3), proving value preservation, exponential reduction of uninformative instances, and monotonicity of expected pool value under reasonable assumptions.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Extensive experiments across 6 image datasets, 3 modern vision backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), and multiple setup variations (imbalance, distribution shift, audio spectrogram classification). The method demonstrates consistent improvements over 8 individual strategies and 4 ensemble methods.

Versatile plug-and-play property: The paper convincingly demonstrates that progressive filtering functions as an effective preconditioning step that can boost the performance of even external/weak AL algorithms (e.g., BAIT, Coreset).
weaknesses: Computational overhead: Applying $M$ strategies over $J$ draws across $R$ rounds requires $M \times J \times R$ strategy calls per AL cycle (e.g., $8 \times 10 \times 5 = 400$ evaluations). Although subsampling with ratio $\alpha$ and multi-core parallelization mitigate this, the acquisition time and compute footprint remain substantially higher than standard single-strategy active learning.

Strong theoretical assumptions: Theorem 3 relies on the assumption that all strategies consistently rank instances in concordance with their true marginal value ($V(x) > V(y) \implies p_{m,r}(x) \ge p_{m,r}(y)$). In realistic AL settings, individual heuristics frequently suffer from failure modes (e.g., oversampling outliers or redundant noisy clusters), which challenges this monotonicity assumption in practice.

Ensemble sensitivity and equal weighting: Because progressive filtering relies on the union of strategy proposals, it lacks an adaptive mechanism to downweight or filter out degenerate heuristics, making candidate pool quality inherently dependent on manual curation of the ensemble set $S$.
